## Suspension of Complaint

### Section 241.1: Suspension of Complaint by the Board

Section 241.1 outlines the circumstances under which the Board can suspend consideration of a complaint.
"If the Board is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This indicates that the Board's power to suspend a complaint is triggered by a need for the complainant to fulfill certain obligations. The Board must be convinced that these measures are necessary before it can halt the review process.

Section 241.1 further details the notification process when the Board suspends consideration.
"If the Board suspends consideration of a complaint, the Board shall notify the complainant in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the complainant must take; and (b) the period within which they must take those measures." This emphasizes the Board's obligation to inform the complainant of the required actions and the timeframe for their completion.

### Section 246.2: Suspension of Complaint by the Board (Similar to 241.1)

Section 246.2 presents a very similar provision to Section 241.1 regarding the Board's power to suspend a complaint.
"If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This mirrors the language of Section 241.1, highlighting the need for the complainant to take steps before the Board can proceed.

Section 246.2 also specifies the content of the Board's written notice to the complainant.
"If the Board suspends a complaint, the Board shall notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." This reinforces the Board's duty to clearly communicate the complainant's responsibilities and the deadline for their fulfillment.

### Section 251.01: Making of Complaint - Limitations

Section 251.01 details the circumstances under which an employee can make a complaint and outlines limitations on making multiple complaints based on substantially the same facts.
"An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under any of subsections 240(1), 246.1(1) and 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn." This is a key limitation, preventing employees from repeatedly filing complaints on the same issue. It allows for a single, comprehensive complaint to be pursued.

### Section 251.02: Assistance — Head - Suspension of Complaint

Section 251.02 also addresses the suspension of a complaint, but in the context of the Head's involvement.
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." This is a parallel provision to Section 241.1 and Section 246.2, indicating that the Head has the authority to suspend a complaint if the complainant needs to take certain actions.

Section 251.02 further explains the Head's notification requirements when suspending a complaint.
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." This mirrors the Board's notification obligations in Sections 241.1 and 246.2.

"After receipt of a complaint, the Head may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint." This indicates that the Head can intervene to help the parties reach an agreement, which would likely result in the complaint being suspended and ultimately withdrawn.

individual_results.question: What are the implications for an employee and an employer in terms of contributions to benefits during an employee's leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Implications for Employee and Employer Contributions to Benefits During Medical Leave of Absence

### Entitlement to Benefits During Leave

Section 209.2(1) of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental principle that
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave." This means that an employee on medical leave continues to accrue their benefits as if they were still actively working.

Section 209.2(2) further clarifies the financial responsibility during this leave. It states,
"Where contributions are required from an employee in order for the employee to be entitled to a benefit referred to in subsection (1), the employee is responsible for and must, within a reasonable time, pay those contributions for the period of any leave of absence under this Division unless, before taking leave or within a reasonable time thereafter, the employee notifies the employer of the employee’s intention to discontinue contributions during that period." This highlights the employee's obligation to continue making contributions, but also provides a mechanism for them to do so if they plan to discontinue them.

Section 209.2(2.1) addresses the employer's corresponding responsibility. It specifies,
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (1) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s leave of absence under this Division in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not on leave unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time." This ensures that the employer maintains its contribution level, mirroring what it would do if the employee were still working.

### Failure to Pay Contributions

Section 209.2(3) outlines the consequences of the employee failing to make contributions. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating the pension, health and disability benefits of an employee in respect of whom contributions have not been paid as required by subsections (2) and (2.1), the benefits shall not accumulate during the leave of absence and employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This means that if the employee does not continue making contributions, their benefits will not accumulate during the leave, and their employment history will not be considered continuous.

### Deemed Continuous Employment

Section 209.2(4) provides a mechanism to prevent a loss of benefits due to a temporary lapse in employee contributions. It states,
"For the purposes of calculating benefits of an employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division, other than benefits referred to in subsection (1), employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence." This ensures that the employee's benefits are not negatively impacted if they temporarily stop making contributions but resume them before returning to work.

### Implications for Employer

Section 247.95(1) addresses the employer's obligation to provide notice of any changes to wages or benefits during a leave of absence. It states,
"If, during a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the wages or benefits of the group of employees of which an employee is a member are changed as part of a plan to reorganize the industrial establishment in which that group is employed, the employee is entitled, on reinstatement under this section, to receive the wages and benefits in respect of that employment that that employee would have been entitled to receive had that employee been working when the reorganization took place." This highlights the employer's responsibility to inform the employee of any such changes.

Section 247.96(1) prohibits employers from taking into account an employee's reserve force membership or intention to take or have taken a leave of absence in any decision to promote or train them. This ensures that employees on leave are not disadvantaged in their career progression.

individual_results.question: What information must an employer provide to redundant employees in writing, and by when, after giving notice of termination under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code?
individual_results.answer:
## Information to Redundant Employees in Writing

### Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 shall give each redundant employee, as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

This passage directly answers the question by identifying the required information. An employer must provide a written statement to each redundant employee. This statement must detail their accrued vacation benefits, wages, severance pay (if applicable), and any other benefits and pay earned during their employment with the company. The deadline for providing this statement is
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee..." This timeframe ensures that redundant employees have adequate time to review the information and understand their entitlements.

### Section 222(1) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 222(1) further elaborates on the information that must be provided, stating:
"The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee shall, on request of any member of the committee, forthwith provide the committee with such personal information relating to any redundant employee as the committee may reasonably require for its work."

While this section focuses on information for the joint planning committee, it reinforces the obligation to provide redundant employees with comprehensive information about their employment terms. The phrase
"...such personal information relating to any redundant employee as the committee may reasonably require for its work." suggests a broader scope than just the specific items listed in section 213(2). It implies that the committee may request additional details relevant to their planning efforts, and the employer is obligated to furnish them.

### Section 212(1) of the Canada Labour Code

Section 212(1) outlines the initial notification requirements, which are a precursor to providing the written statement. It mandates that an employer must give notice to the Head, in writing, of their intention to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees at least 16 weeks before the first termination date. This notice sets the stage for the subsequent provision of the detailed written statement to the redundant employees.

In summary, an employer must provide redundant employees in writing a statement detailing their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the company, no later than two weeks before the date of termination, after giving notice of termination under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code. This information is a crucial component of the group termination process, ensuring that affected employees are informed of their entitlements and have time to plan for their future.

individual_results.question: Can a request for review of a notice of violation be escalated to a higher authority, and under what circumstances?
individual_results.answer:
## Escalation of a Notice of Violation Review

### Section 281: Request for Review

Section 281 establishes the initial step in escalating a notice of violation review. It states:
"A person or a department that is served with a notice of violation may, within 30 days after the day on which the notice is served, or within any longer period that the Head allows, make a request, in the manner prescribed by regulation, to the Head for a review of the penalty or the facts of the alleged violation, or both."
This passage directly answers the question by confirming that a request for review of a notice of violation *can* be escalated to the Head. It specifies the timeframe within which such a request must be made and the method by which it should be submitted.

### Section 283: Head's Review Process

Section 283 details the Head's responsibilities upon receiving a review request. It mentions the Head's obligation to "conduct the review of the notice of violation."
"On receipt of a request for review made under section 281, the Head shall conduct the review of the notice of violation."
This indicates that the Head is the first authority to examine the notice of violation and make a determination.

### Section 283: Treating a Request as an Appeal

Section 283 further clarifies the escalation process by allowing the Head to treat a review request as an appeal.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal, in which case the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."
This is a crucial point as it outlines the circumstances under which the review request is not just a reconsideration by the Head, but a formal appeal to the Board. The Head must inform the applicant of this treatment and forward the request to the Board.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal, in which case the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."
This quote is central to understanding the escalation path. It explicitly states that the Head can escalate the review request to the Board by treating it as an appeal.

### Section 251.101: Review and Appeal - Request for Review

Section 251.101 also addresses the escalation of a notice of violation review. It mentions that an employer or a director of a corporation can send a written request with reasons to the Head for a review of the Head’s decision.
"An employer or a director of a corporation is not permitted to request a review of a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the payment order and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the payment order in accordance with subsection 251.131(1), subject to, in the case of a director, the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18. Marginal note: Security (2.1) The Head may allow an employer or a director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (2). Marginal note: Review (3) On receipt of the request for review, the Head may, in writing, (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the payment order or the compliance order; or (b) confirm the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance, or rescind the notice, in which case the Head shall re-examine the complaint."
While this section primarily focuses on the Head's response to the review request, it confirms that the Head is the initial authority to escalate the review to the Board if deemed appropriate.

### Section 251.11: Right of Appeal

Section 251.11 outlines the right of appeal from a decision made under subsection (3) of Section 251.101.
"Subject to the right of appeal under section 251.11, the decision made under subsection (3) is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court."
This passage confirms that the Board's decision on a review request is final and conclusive, with no further appeal available. However, it also acknowledges the right of appeal from the Head's initial review decision under section 251.11.

In summary, a request for review of a notice of violation *can* be escalated to a higher authority, specifically the Board, under two primary circumstances: first, if the Head considers the review request as an appeal, and second, if the Head's initial review decision is appealed under section 251.11. The Head is the initial authority to make this escalation.

individual_results.question: In cases where an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, who bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did or did not occur?
individual_results.answer:
## Burden of Proof in Complaints Against Employees

### Section 133: Complaint to Board - Burden of Proof

Section 133 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly addresses the burden of proof when an employee complains about an employer's action in contravention of section 147.
"A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be, in relation to the matter that is the subject-matter of the complaint." This indicates a prerequisite for filing a complaint under section 133. However, the subsequent provision clarifies the burden of proof.
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint." This states that if the Board proceeds with the complaint, it will determine whether the contravention actually occurred.
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party." This is a crucial passage. It establishes that the very act of filing a complaint under section 133 is prima facie evidence that the contravention occurred. Therefore, if a party to the complaint proceedings denies the contravention, the burden of proof shifts to that party to demonstrate that it did not happen.

### Section 6.2: General Burden of Proof in Proceedings

Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code provides a general rule regarding the burden of proof in proceedings under this Part, excluding prosecutions.
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This passage directly answers the question by stating that if an employer in a proceeding under this Part (other than a prosecution) alleges that a person is not their employee, the employer bears the burden of proving that the person is not their employee.

### Section 123.3: General Burden of Proof in Proceedings

Section 123.3 of the Canada Labour Code further reinforces the general burden of proof rule.
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer." This section reiterates the same rule as Section 6.2, applying it to proceedings under Part IV that are related to this Part.

### Section 123.2: Presumption of Employee Status

Section 123.2 establishes a presumption that a person paid remuneration by an employer is their employee, unless the contrary is proven by the employer.
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer." This presumption is a significant factor in determining the burden of proof. It means that the employer has the initial burden of proving that the person is *not* their employee. If the employer fails to do so, the presumption stands, and the employee does not have to prove their employment status.

### Section 147: Disciplinary Action - Burden of Proof

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the types of disciplinary actions an employer cannot take against an employee for exercising their rights under this Part. While it doesn't directly address the burden of proof in complaints, it highlights the importance of the employee having a valid right that they exercised.
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off or demote an employee, impose a financial or other penalty on an employee, or refuse to pay an employee remuneration in respect of any period that the employee would, but for the exercise of the employee’s rights under this Part, have worked, or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part." This section underscores that the employee's exercise of their rights is protected from retaliation, implying that the employer would bear the burden of proving that the disciplinary action was not retaliatory.

individual_results.question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work for an employee in a week be adjusted or have exceptions?
individual_results.answer:
## Conditions for Adjusting or Exempting Maximum Hours of Work

### Excess Hour Permits
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This indicates that an employer can exceed the standard 48-hour work week under specific emergency circumstances. However, this is not an automatic adjustment; it requires a permit and a subsequent report to the Head and, if applicable, a trade union.

### Averaging Plans
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks. As such, standard and maximum hours would be calculated across a period of 2 or more weeks rather than on a daily or weekly basis." This section details how employers can average an employee's hours over a longer period (2 or more weeks) to account for variations in work schedule. This averaging allows for exceeding the 48-hour maximum on some weeks while staying within the 40-hour average for the two-week period.

### Collective Agreements
"Section 172 (1) An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union." This passage highlights that if an employee is covered by a collective agreement, the employer can adjust the work schedule to exceed the 48-hour maximum, provided the average hours over two or more weeks do not exceed 48 and the change is agreed upon in writing by both the employer and the trade union.

### Modified Work Schedules
"Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work. Examples of modified work schedules include:   compressed work weeks flexible hours of work   Note: you can also request modified work schedules under the right to request flexible work arrangements. For more information, please consult the Flexible Work Arrangements web page.  If you have a modified work schedule:   your standard hours of work for a period of 2 or more weeks cannot exceed an average of 40 hours in a week  the maximum hours for the same period cannot exceed an average of 48 hours in a week your employer must pay overtime when  your daily or weekly hours exceed those established under the modified work schedule. Overtime must also be paid when your hours exceed an average of 40 hours in a week where the schedule consists of 2 or more weeks  If you are a student intern, your employer may establish a modified work schedule with your approval. This schedule can exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. However, it cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks." This section outlines the conditions under which modified work schedules can be established. It specifies that the average hours over two or more weeks cannot exceed 40 hours, and the maximum hours for that period cannot exceed 48 hours. Overtime must be paid when these averages are exceeded. It also mentions that modified work schedules can be established for student interns with their approval, but they cannot exceed 40 hours per week averaged over a period of 2 or more weeks.

### Exemptions from and Modifications to Hours of Work Provisions Regulations
"Regulations set out exemptions from or modifications to what maximum hours of work is for certain classes of employees:  drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..." This indicates that there are specific exemptions from the 48-hour maximum hours rule for certain professions and industries, as detailed in the relevant regulations.
